permits.name: Form your legal entity with the Colorado Secretary of State (LLC / corporation)
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Secretary of State – Business Division
permits.notes: Online filing is cheap and usually effective immediately: Articles of Organization (LLC) or Articles of Incorporation cost $50. A trade name statement is $20 if the restaurant name differs from the entity name. The periodic report is $25 a year, or $50 if late. Do this first, since the EIN, state sales tax license, Denver tax account and liquor applications all need the exact entity name.

permits.name: Colorado retail sales tax license (MyBizColorado)
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Taxation Division
permits.notes: Each location needs a license. Single-location businesses apply through MyBizColorado, and businesses with multiple locations file the paper CR 0100. The cost is a prorated license fee ($4–$16 depending on when you apply) plus a one-time $50 deposit, refunded automatically after you remit $50 of state sales tax. The state rate is 2.9% on food, drink and lodging. Home-rule cities such as Denver collect their own sales tax and need a separate city license. Retail food and liquor licenses require this license.

permits.name: Unemployment insurance employer account (CDLE)
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment (CDLE) – Unemployment Insurance Employer Services
permits.notes: Register through MyBizColorado or MyUI Employer+ once you are paying wages to at least one Colorado employee (paper form UITL-100 also accepted). Most employers become liable after paying $1,500 in a quarter or employing someone in 20 weeks. New non-construction employers pay a 1.70% introductory rate for 2027. Premium and wage reports are due quarterly.

permits.name: Workers' compensation insurance (from the first employee)
permits.issuing_agency: Private carrier (e.g. Pinnacol Assurance), regulated by CDLE Division of Workers' Compensation
permits.notes: Required from the first employee, whether part-time, full-time or family. Coverage comes from a private carrier or approved self-insurance, since there is no state fund. You can't deduct any of the premium from wages. Operating uninsured risks fines of up to $500 per day, possible shutdown, and paying claims yourself plus a 25% penalty. Licensing authorities and landlords commonly ask for the certificate.

permits.name: Local licensing authority approval of the liquor license (city or county – filed first)
permits.issuing_agency: Your city or county local licensing authority (clerk / liquor board), under the Colorado Liquor Code
permits.notes: Colorado uses dual licensing: you file the state and local applications with the city or county first, and the state won't issue until the local authority approves. New applicants typically must show the 'needs and desires' of the neighborhood (petitions, witness testimony) at a noticed public hearing, and the local authority usually runs the background check. Local application fees run up to $1,000 plus a $75 local license fee. Denver's process is covered by the Denver liquor entries.
permits.stall_risk: Hearing dates, posting periods and neighborhood opposition set the timeline. A thin needs-and-desires petition or an organized neighborhood objection can push the hearing or lead to denial. Start the petition the week the lease is signed.

permits.name: Hotel & Restaurant liquor license (full liquor with meals) – state approval
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Liquor Enforcement Division (LED)
permits.notes: This is the standard full-bar license for restaurants. You need a real kitchen serving meals, and at least 25% of gross income must come from food. The state charges a $1,100 application fee ($1,200 with concurrent state/local review) plus the $500 license fee. Hotel & Restaurant licenses aren't capped, but the local authority must approve first. Managers who aren't owners register with the city and state for $30 each. Denver applicants: see the Denver Hotel & Restaurant entry, which covers both city and state steps.

permits.name: Tavern liquor license (full-liquor bar) – state approval
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Liquor Enforcement Division (LED)
permits.notes: This license is for bars that serve beer, wine and spirits with only sandwiches and light snacks required. Fees are $1,100 for the state application plus the $500 state license. A 500-ft distance restriction from schools applies, and local authorities may deny a new tavern that adds to an undue concentration. A brewery-restaurant brewing on site uses the separate Brew Pub license ($750 state) instead.

permits.name: Beer & Wine liquor license (on-premises) – state approval
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Liquor Enforcement Division (LED)
permits.notes: This license covers beer and wine by the drink for cafes, wine bars and casual restaurants. Fees are a $1,100 state application plus a $351.25 state license fee in a city ($436.25 in unincorporated county areas). It goes through the same local-first process and neighborhood needs-and-desires showing as full-liquor licenses, so the savings are in fees, not time. Breweries and brewpubs use Brew Pub or manufacturer licenses instead.

permits.name: Lodging Facility liquor license (hotels; formerly 'Lodging & Entertainment') – state approval
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Liquor Enforcement Division (LED)
permits.notes: The old Lodging & Entertainment class has been split into separate Lodging Facility and Entertainment Facility licenses ($1,100 state application plus $500 license each). A hotel whose restaurant meets the meal and food-revenue rules can instead hold a Hotel & Restaurant license, with optional premises ($100 each) for pool bars and event spaces. Minibars need a separate permit.

permits.name: Responsible Vendor alcohol server training (voluntary penalty mitigation)
permits.issuing_agency: LED-approved Responsible Vendor trainers (Colorado Liquor Enforcement Division, Regulation 47-605)
permits.notes: This is not required by the state. However, if your servers and managers complete an LED-approved Responsible Vendor course, a first sale-to-minor or over-service violation is treated more leniently. Recertification is every two years. Courses cover ID checks, visible intoxication and takeout/delivery rules, and some trainers offer live-streamed classes. Many local authorities and insurers expect it.

permits.name: Retail Food Establishment license (county / local public health agency)
permits.issuing_agency: Local public health agency for your county (CDPHE directly in 9 small counties)
permits.notes: Colorado restaurants and food trucks are licensed by the county or district public health agency under the state's retail food rules. CDPHE licenses directly only in Clear Creek, Dolores, Gilpin, Moffat, Ouray, Park, Pitkin (outside Aspen), Rio Blanco and San Juan. There, plan review costs a $155 application fee plus up to $580, with comments within 14 days. Every agency requires a Colorado sales tax license, and you can begin construction once you have the plan approval letter. Denver issues its own license (see the Denver Retail Food entry).

permits.name: Food safety manager / person-in-charge training
permits.issuing_agency: ANSI-accredited exam provider (ServSafe, NRFSP, Prometric, etc.); rules by CDPHE and local health agencies
permits.notes: Colorado's retail food rules require a person in charge who can demonstrate food-safety knowledge. A Certified Food Protection Manager isn't uniformly mandated statewide, but some local agencies (including Denver) expect one. Certifying one manager through an accredited exam satisfies every Colorado jurisdiction and helps at the pre-opening inspection. Check your county agency's employee food-handler expectations too.

permits.name: State sales tax on lodging + state-collected county lodging / marketing district taxes
permits.issuing_agency: Colorado Department of Revenue – Taxation Division
permits.notes: Colorado charges its 2.9% sales tax on the full room charge, including cleaning and other room fees, for stays under 30 days. Rooms let to a permanent resident under a written agreement of 30+ days are exempt. You collect it under your state sales tax license, and DOR also administers county lodging taxes (Form DR 1485) and local marketing district taxes (DR 1490) where they apply. City lodging taxes, such as Denver's lodger's tax, are filed with the city.
